bridges.description: Support the existence of the classical-theist God as necessary unlimited being with intellect, will, and perfect goodness.
Infer a necessary ground from contingent reality.
Infer a timeless personal cause from a finite universe.
Infer perfect goodness from objective moral facts.
Withhold classical theism unless its premises and comparative advantage are established.
Challenge contingency, beginning, fine-tuning, and moral premises.
Require comparison with contrary evidence and alternatives.
Treat nonbelief and suffering as probabilistic evidence.

sections.title: Burdens and inference method
sections.rationale: The parties dispute the negative burden, premise standards, deduction, and probabilistic comparison.

sections.title: Contingency and necessary being
sections.rationale: Horn's proposed ultimate ground and Lataster's modal objections form a central route.

sections.title: Finite origin and time
sections.rationale: The beginning argument and eternalist alternatives remain distinct from contingency.

sections.title: Fine-tuning and design
sections.rationale: Life-permitting constants generate a design inference and focused probability objections.

sections.title: Morality, suffering, and hiddenness
sections.rationale: Moral facts support perfect goodness, while suffering and hiddenness supply contrary evidence.

sections.title: Rival God concepts
sections.rationale: The motion turns on whether the routes reach classical theism rather than another supernatural concept.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The affirmative answers yes and targets an immaterial, pure, unlimited being grounding all existence.
moves.warrant: Science does not settle every existence question, while philosophy addresses fundamental and immaterial reality.
moves.inference: Philosophical arguments can address the specified classical-theist target.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage states Horn's answer, burden, and definition, ending when he introduces the four routes structuring his case.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the most basic reality that grounds all of existence
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator hands the opening to Horn and first-person continuity is uninterrupted.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the target and affirmative burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the affirmative conclusion and target.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The contingent universe requires an explanation terminating in necessary reality.
moves.warrant: Horn invokes sufficient reason, argues the universe could fail to exist, and rejects an infinite contingent regress.
moves.inference: The terminus is identified with pure existence or unlimited being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves the complete route from sufficient reason through contingency and rejection of a contingent regress to the claimed ground.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there must be a reality that is necessary
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the uninterrupted opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: This central route later supports uniqueness.

burdenContact.rationale: It infers a necessary ground from contingent existence.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: The universe began and therefore has a cause beyond physical reality.
moves.warrant: Horn appeals to causal intuition, reported science, and the alleged impossibility of traversing an infinite past.
moves.inference: The cause is said to be immaterial, eternal, powerful, and personal.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete span includes the causal premise, scientific and philosophical support, and all inferred attributes; each stage is disputed later.
moves.attributionRationale: Horn remains the sole opening speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It anchors the later time dispute.

burdenContact.rationale: It states and supports the beginning-to-cause inference.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Life-permitting constants are better explained by design than chance or necessity.
moves.warrant: Horn reports extreme sensitivity, argues chance is improbable, and says necessity is undemonstrated.
moves.inference: An agent setting early conditions is offered as explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves Horn's full comparison of chance, necessity, and agency for life-permitting order.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the independent design route.

burdenContact.rationale: It links order to purposive agency.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: Objective moral facts, equal dignity, and intrinsic prohibitions are explained by perfect goodness.
moves.warrant: Horn defends moral realism, argues unequal capacities cannot ground equal rights, and contrasts intrinsic wrongs with outcome-only rules.
moves.inference: A perfectly good source grounds moral facts and value.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The long span preserves moral realism, equal dignity, intrinsic evil, and the concluding perfect-goodness inference as linked stages of one argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It reaches perfect goodness rather than generic cause.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives the moral grounding inference.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: As an agnostic non-theist, Lataster challenges the specified case without proving universal divine nonexistence.
moves.warrant: He distinguishes non-theism from denial, identifies classical attributes, and says disputed premises and generic supernatural conclusions need support.
moves.inference: The affirmative must establish its specified God while the negative may challenge premises and alternatives.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage contains Lataster's complete burden clarification and identification of classical theism before individual replies begin.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I am agnostic you can call me agnostic if you like
moves.attributionRationale: Lataster is the announced opening speaker.

burdenContact.rationale: It defines withholding the specified conclusion.

responseComponents.description: Rejects Horn's proposed negative burden while accepting the classical-theist target.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Neither the world's contingency nor divine necessity has been established.
moves.warrant: Lataster says the world might be necessary and divine necessity cannot simply be assumed.
moves.inference: The route needs further warrant for both modal premises.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This narrow passage is the complete direct reply to contingency and necessity before the beginning argument is addressed.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't actually know that the world is contingent

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the unsupported modal premises.

responseComponents.description: Disputes the universe's contingency and the ground's necessity.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Creation from nothing is not established, and the beginning argument depends on a contested theory of time.
moves.warrant: Lataster distinguishes expansion from creation and later clarifies that eternalist theories generally remain live without popularity proving them.
moves.inference: The finite-past premise cannot be treated as settled.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the complete opening objection to scientific creation claims and the philosophical time premise.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Big Bang doesn't actually prove that the Universe came into existence
moves.attributionRationale: Ownership is clear, but captions corrupt names and technical wording.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify scientific names and creation terminology before publication.
moves.importanceRationale: It contests the causal route's beginning premise.

burdenContact.rationale: It marks beginning and time theory as live.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes expansion from creation and raises eternalism.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Design does not win merely because chance and necessity are presented as unsupported.
moves.warrant: Lataster says the ordering is arbitrary, necessity remains live, and other constants might permit other life.
moves.inference: Fine-tuning requires comparative probabilities rather than design by default.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the full opening reply from the alleged default inference through necessity and alternative-life objections.

burdenContact.rationale: It requires comparison of chance, necessity, and design.

responseComponents.description: Challenges elimination of chance and necessity and assumptions about life.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Morality's dependence on God is unestablished, while nonbelief and suffering count probabilistically against classical theism.
moves.warrant: Lataster says moral facts might be absent or natural and hiddenness and suffering fit naturalism or different gods better.
moves.inference: The evidence shifts comparative probability without logically disproving every God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This long span preserves the moral-premise objections, method qualification, and both positive evidential routes as the complete answer to perfect goodness.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it doesn't prove that God doesn't exist
moves.importanceRationale: It joins the direct moral reply to his main contrary evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It presents hiddenness and suffering as probabilistic evidence.

responseComponents.description: Challenges moral realism, divine grounding, and perfect goodness.
Tests the specified God against nonbelief.

moves.speaker: Raphael Lataster
moves.claim: Even conditionally granting supernaturalism and monotheism leaves many rival God concepts live.
moves.warrant: Lataster says simplicity is unquantified, rivals may add fewer assumptions, and some fit hiddenness or suffering better.
moves.inference: Generic supernatural evidence does not establish classical theism without comparison.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span is required because Lataster constructs polytheistic, deistic, quasi-deistic, alternative-monotheistic, pantheistic, and mixed families with distinct reasons.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are infinitely many supernaturalistic Alternatives
moves.attributionRationale: Continuity is clear, but technical labels are corrupted.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify God-concept labels before exact publication.
moves.importanceRationale: This is his central rival-concept argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies rivals the affirmative must distinguish.

responseComponents.description: Says necessary reality does not select classical theism.
Treats a cause as compatible with rivals.
Treats design as compatible with other agents.

moves.speaker: Trent Horn
moves.claim: An ultimate necessary explanation cannot be limited or divided, and uniform order points to one source.
moves.warrant: Horn says limits require explanation, plurality compromises ultimacy, pantheism identifies cause with effect, and perfect goodness excludes indifferent deism.
moves.inference: Contingency, order, and morality narrow supernaturalism toward classical monotheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete rebuttal preserves limitation, uniqueness, order, pantheism, and deism replies as linked narrowing steps.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the cause of reality cannot be limited in any way
moves.attributionRationale: Horn is the announced rebuttal speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Horn's principal narrowing answer.

burdenContact.rationale: It says why the routes reach the specified God.

responseComponents.description: Offers uniqueness, order, cause-effect distinction, and goodness against rivals.

omissions.reason: Excluded introduction, biographies, format, and handoff.
Excluded audience Q&A and closing transition; closing references do not import it.
Later replies, cross-examination, and closings repeat, clarify, or synthesize selected routes; rhetorical characterization and peripheral examples are omitted.

coverageAudit.qualificationPreservation: Conditional grants are not beliefs; hiddenness and suffering are probabilistic, not logical disproof; the limb example may not evidence God; eternalism is broader than B theory and popularity is not proof; Horn's definition, infinity, moral knowledge, hiddenness reasons, and convergence distinctions are preserved.

speakerAttributionReview.handoffs: Moderator announcements and first-person continuity identify turns; auxiliary text confirms ambiguous transitions.
speakerAttributionReview.explicitAddressees: Direct names identify reply targets only.
speakerAttributionReview.firstPersonContinuity: Opening and rebuttal passages have stable continuity.
mixedSpans: Interrupted cross-examination is not selected separately; required qualifications are preserved in the audit.
Auxiliary closing text confirms terminology context without replacing captions.
uncertainties: Captions corrupt names, technical labels, and numbers.
The closing self-correction and corrupted de facto phrase support no adverse inference.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: Every section contains one load-bearing move per side.
